The must-sees

  • Abbey of Saint-Victor

    Church

    The abbey was founded in the 5th century, and its crypts hold early Christian sarcophagi. Every February at Candlemas it blesses and sells navettes, boat-shaped biscuits.

    Look for: In the crypt, find the dark wooden statue of Notre-Dame de Confession, the Black Virgin carried in procession at Candlemas.

  • Château d’If

    Fortress

    François I had the fort built in the early 16th century, and it soon became a state prison. Alexandre Dumas made it the jail of the Count of Monte Cristo.

    Look for: In the cells, look for names, dates and ships scratched into the walls by prisoners.

  • Cité Radieuse

    Building · 1952

    Le Corbusier completed it in 1952, with shops and a hotel on its inner street and a school on the roof. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing of his work.

    Look for: At the foot of the building, find the Modulor pressed into the concrete: Le Corbusier’s raised-arm figure that sets the building’s proportions.

  • Fort Saint-Jean

    Fortress

    Louis XIV had the fort built in the 1660s around older towers, one of them left by the Knights of St John who gave it its name. Its walkways and gardens are now part of the MuCEM.

    Look for: Across the harbour mouth stands Fort Saint-Nicolas, its twin, built at the same time.

  • La Canebière

    Landmark

    Its name comes from the Provençal word for hemp, which was once made into rope nearby. For sailors it was the street that stood for Marseille itself.

  • La Vieille Charité

    Culture

    Pierre Puget designed this 17th-century almshouse, built to take in the city’s poor. Restored in the late 20th century, it now holds museums of Mediterranean archaeology and of African, Oceanic and Amerindian art.

    Look for: Look up at the chapel dome: Puget made it oval rather than round, unusual for its time.

  • Le Panier

    Neighbourhood

    The Greek city began on this hill, making it Marseille’s oldest quarter. Much of the area just below was destroyed in 1943, but these upper streets survived.

    Look for: In the Panier, Place de Lenche is thought to stand on the site of the Greek city’s marketplace.

  • Marseille Cathedral

    Church · 1893

    Built between 1852 and 1893 to designs by Léon Vaudoyer, it is one of the largest churches built in France in the 19th century. Part of the small Romanesque Old Major still stands beside it.

    Look for: Compare the stripes: green stone from Florence banded with white stone from Calissanne, near Marseille.

  • MuCEM

    Museum · 2013

    The museum of Mediterranean civilisations opened in 2013 in a building by Rudy Ricciotti. A slim footbridge links its roof terrace to Fort Saint-Jean across the water.

    Look for: Follow the ramps that wind up between the glass walls and the concrete lattice; the light through the lace changes all day.

  • Notre-Dame de la Garde

    Church · 1864

    Designed by Henri-Jacques Espérandieu, it was consecrated in 1864 on the city’s highest point. Marseillais call it la Bonne Mère, the good mother who watches over sailors and the port.

    Look for: Inside, the walls are covered with ex-votos: small paintings of ships in storms and model boats hung from the ceiling, thanks from sailors and their families.

  • Old Port

    Waterfront

    Greek settlers from Phocaea founded Massalia on this inlet around 600 BC. It stayed the city’s working harbour until the larger docks to the north opened in the 19th century.

    Look for: On the quay at the head of the harbour, stand under Norman Foster’s mirrored steel canopy and find yourself upside down above the crowd.

  • Palais Longchamp

    Palace · 1869

    Henri-Jacques Espérandieu designed it to celebrate water from the Durance brought by the Canal de Marseille. One wing holds the fine arts museum, the other the natural history museum.

    Look for: In the central fountain, a woman stands for the river Durance, drawn by four bulls of the Camargue.

How it works

  1. Open Wizzy in Marseille and tap Start walk, or pick a ready-made walk.
  2. Put your phone in your pocket. Wizzy runs in the background, even with the screen locked.
  3. When you pass a place, you get a ping. Open it for the story, or keep walking.

Every place you see gets stamped in your Marseille passport. Your location stays on your phone. No ads, no tracking.
